claims.text: Controlled surface segregation concentrates lower-cohesive-energy species at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface segregation of lower-cohesive-energy species reduces the local cohesive energy at the nanoparticle surface.
Reduced local surface cohesive energy causes an earlier premelting transition.
Surface compositional heterogeneity broadens the premelting transition relative to a homogeneous surface composition.
The compared nanoparticles can be prepared with identical overall composition and size.
A kinetically trapped HEA nanoparticle state can exhibit a uniform surface composition.
Controlled annealing will induce surface segregation in one nanoparticle set.
Rapid quenching will preserve a homogeneous nanoparticle surface composition.
Cu has a comparatively weak cohesive contribution because its d-band is fully occupied and therefore tends to segregate to the HEA surface.
Pd can segregate to the surface of a Pd-Cu-Pt-Ni-Co HEA.
Lower local surface cohesive energy reduces the energy barrier for atomic mobility.
Enhanced surface atomic mobility initiates premelting at a lower temperature than on a uniformly composed surface.
Annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will have an earlier premelting onset than homogeneous quenched nanoparticles.
Annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will exhibit a broader premelting and melting temperature range than homogeneous quenched nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism should hold for HEA nanoparticles approximately 5–10 nm in size.
The quantitative premelting-temperature shift and melting-range change may depend on alloy composition and synthesis conditions.

A statistically indistinguishable premelting onset and melting range between confirmed segregated and homogeneous samples would falsify the proposed governing role of surface compositional heterogeneity under the tested conditions.
